title: Layers: Envelopes in Envelopes
objective: After this level you can explain how internet protocols wrap data in layers, each layer doing one job for the one above.
summary: Internet protocols stack four layers (application, transport, internet, link); sending wraps data in each layer's header, and the receiver unwraps them in reverse.

cards.headline: Your message leaves your phone inside envelopes inside envelopes.
cards.body: By the time a chat message goes out, several pieces of software have each wrapped it in a label of their own. Each does one job and passes it on. Unwrapping them tells you how the whole internet is organized.

cards.headline: Four layers, four jobs
cards.body: The internet's rulebook, from 1989, stacks four layers. Application: the program's own message, such as an email. Transport: TCP or UDP, carrying it end to end between programs. Internet: IP, moving it from the source computer to the destination computer across networks. Link: the rules of whatever local network it's crossing right now.

cards.headline: Wrap on the way down, unwrap on the way up
cards.body: Each layer wraps what it gets from above with its own header. TCP adds port numbers, ordering information and a checksum, making a segment. IP adds the sending and receiving IP addresses. The link layer adds a header and an error-checking footer, making a frame. On arrival, each layer strips off the header its twin added at the sender and passes the rest up.

cards.headline: Four layers or seven?
cards.body: You may also meet the OSI model, set out by the International Organization for Standardization, which splits the same work into seven layers. The internet's own rulebook uses four: its application layer does the jobs of OSI's top two layers, called presentation and application.

mascot.line: People mix these two up all the time. OSI is a seven-layer model; the internet itself was built on four. Same idea, different slicing.

cards.headline: Layers: unwrapped
learned: Four layers: application, transport, internet, link
Each layer adds its own header on the way down
The receiver strips them off on the way up
OSI slices the same work into seven layers

questions.prompt: Put the internet's four layers in order, from the program's message down to the local network.
questions.explanation: From the top: the application layer holds the program's message, transport carries it end to end, internet moves it between computers, and link handles the local network.

questions.prompt: How does the receiving computer get the original message back out of a frame?

options.label: It keeps only the last byte and throws away the rest of the frame
options.rationale: The message is inside the headers, not at the end.

options.label: Each layer strips off its own header and passes the rest up
The sender emails a clean copy of the message separately
options.rationale: The message arrives inside the frame itself.

options.label: The last router unwraps everything before handing it over
options.rationale: Unwrapping happens layer by layer at the receiver.

questions.explanation: Each layer removes the header its counterpart added at the sender, until the application gets the original message.

questions.prompt: The link layer wraps a packet in a frame. Which addresses on that frame does a Level 31 switch read?

options.label: Domain names
options.rationale: Names are looked up by DNS before sending.

options.label: Port numbers
options.rationale: Ports are in the TCP header, deeper inside.

options.label: Sequence numbers
options.rationale: Those are TCP's, used by the two ends.

questions.explanation: A switch reads the sender and destination MAC addresses on each frame to learn ports and forward it.
